source.title: The Changing DNA of Serious and Organised Crime: EU Serious and Organised Crime Threat Assessment 2025 (EU-SOCTA)

summary: GOLDEN LABEL, hand-drafted against the PDF. Europol's four-yearly strategic assessment of serious and organised crime in the EU, framed around three dynamics: destabilising society (including as proxies for hybrid threat actors), nurtured online, and accelerated by AI. Financial-crime content sits in the cross-cutting tactics chapter (criminal finances and money laundering; criminal exploitation of legal business structures; corruption) and in the crime-area chapter's sections on fraud against the financial interest of the EU (customs import fraud, VAT/MTIC carousel fraud, excise fraud) and sanctions evasion. It describes cash-intensive businesses, money mules, layering through shell companies, cryptocurrency laundering via mixers, chain hopping, privacy coins and DeFi (ChipMixer case), professional launderers and money brokers running parallel financial systems, hawala, free trade zones, trade misinvoicing, and trade-based sanctions evasion of strategic goods to Russia and Belarus through front companies, falsified documents and transhipment via the Eurasian Economic Union and the Caucasus, with sanctioned actors retaining beneficial ownership of corporate structures. Names the ChipMixer, JuicyFields, LockBit, Dutch military-goods export and EUR 297 million VAT fraud cases.

citations.quote: Criminals often use cash-intensive businesses—such as restaurants, hotels, car washes—to mix illicit funds with the businesses’ legitimate income.

Three types of businesses are particularly affected by criminal infiltration or abuse: construction and real estate, cash-intensive businesses (particularly hospitality), and logistics (i.e. transport and import/export companies).
Increasingly, young and vulnerable people are recruited, often via social media and gaming platforms, to act as money mules.
Young people are used as money mules, receiving and transferring illicit funds through their bank accounts, often in exchange for a small share of the money.
The second stage, layering, consists of multiple transactions designed to obscure the origin of the funds through a series of transfers, conversions, or purchases.

From the simple use of cash intensive businesses to complex layering techniques via shell companies, from informal value transfer systems to the exploitation of cryptocurrencies, all these techniques serve as crucial components of a parallel financial criminal underworld.

Sanctions evasion relies heavily on a crime-as-a-service model, with criminal enablers playing a central role throughout the supply chain of goods and assets trafficked or illegally transferred to circumvent sanctions.

Criminal networks leverage strategic trade partnerships — including free trade zones (FTZs), shell companies, trade misinvoicing, and opaque supply chains — to launder money, evade sanctions, and finance illicit activities.
Frauds with Russian-origin-sanctioned products may enable the evasion of restrictive trade sanctions, for example, for Russian vodka or Russian oil products.
These illicit exports were allegedly facilitated through front companies and falsified documentation to circumvent trade restrictions.
Legal businesses are infiltrated, and front companies are set up in retail, import-export, transport, or the financial sector for the procurement and shipment of goods or assets.
Countries from the Eurasian Economic Union and the Caucasus play a central role in transhipment.
the procurement of strategic goods increasingly takes place in third countries serving as transit hubs today, particularly in West and Central Asia.
In early 2024, Dutch authorities arrested three individuals for allegedly exporting military-grade goods to Russia, in violation of European Union sanctions.
sanctions evasion may serve broader agendas, including destabilisation — particularly through the proliferation of strategic goods, fuelling military threats.
Sanctioned actors maintain beneficial ownership of corporate structures and influence across Member States and sectors.
more sophisticated methods of money laundering associated with sanctions evasion, based on complex ownership structures, will likely become mainstream.

It is likely that criminal networks increasingly leverage tools such as encrypted communications, anonymised financial transactions, cryptocurrencies and blockchain technologies, and cyber-enabled trade-based money laundering.
modi operandi often involve multiple transactions across various non-EU jurisdictions, exploiting regulatory disparities and creating a labyrinthine trail that challenges financial investigations.
Specific locations in the Middle East and Asia function as global hubs for money laundering.
MTIC fraud in particular inherently relies on complex networks of companies to obscure participant connections, a level of complexity culminating in contra-trading schemes.
Criminals make use of limited liability companies, individual entrepreneurs, and shell companies, which they quickly establish and dissolve.
Multiple false identities were used as countermeasures and the network used shell companies to launder the profits from the illicit trafficking and trade.
Shell or buffer companies, whether infiltrated or set-up, facilitate the exploitation of cross-border VAT systems and VAT refund processes.
For example, front or shell companies may be used to facilitate the movement of illicit or stolen goods or to enable money laundering activities.

Carousel fraud is the most common form of MTIC fraud and involves a circular trading scheme where the same goods are repeatedly imported and exported across multiple Member States, with VAT refunds being claimed for taxes that were never paid.
Criminals use various methods, including undervaluation, misclassification of the category (tariff classification fraud) and false declaration of the origin of goods.
Goods at higher risk of being undervalued include textiles, food, medicines, electronics, vehicles, sugar, shoes, and toys.
Document fraud, such as the misdeclaration of transported goods, is well-established.
They facilitate the acquisition of fraudulent authorisations and documents, often inflating the price of waste, taking a cut, or completely misdescribing it.
divert chemicals from legal trade to illicit drug production facilities, misusing existing legal business structures and mislabelling chemicals.
Further still, a criminal network can infiltrate an LBS at a high level, coercing key high-level individuals within the structure, or set up its own LBS which it fully controls.
The criminal network had a strong cross-border dimension, led by Russian masterminds, with strawmen in Germany and money laundering activities in Cyprus.

typologies.label: Criminal infiltration and abuse of legal business structures

citations.quote: The abuse of legal business structures (LBS) is a multi-functional tool to support, disguise, or facilitate any form of criminal activity and to launder its proceeds.
A large majority makes use of legal business structures as a facilitator to commit their crimes, as a front to disguise them, or as a vehicle for laundering criminal profits.

typologies.label: Cryptocurrency laundering through mixers, chain hopping, privacy coins and DeFi

citations.quote: ChipMixer, an unlicensed cryptocurrency mixer, was taken down in March 2023, for its alleged involvement in money laundering activities.
Chain hopping, for example, involves the switching between different cryptocurrencies to obscure the origin of funds.
These transactions are difficult to trace when well-known coins are exchanged into less known ones or privacy coins like Monero, enhancing anonymity.

typologies.label: Professional money laundering as a service through parallel underground financial systems

citations.quote: Professional money launderers, increasingly with specialised knowledge in digital asset trading, have developed parallel, underground financial systems that operate outside the regulatory frameworks governing legal financial institutions.
Some high-level money brokers occupy pivotal positions within criminal networks, offering extensive, unregulated financial services to multiple criminal networks.
It refers to schemes where a trader imports goods VAT-free from another EU country and sells them domestically, charging VAT to the buyer but failing to remit this tax to the authorities.
A complex VAT fraud scheme, involving the trade of popular electronic goods, resulted in an estimated VAT loss of EUR 297 million.

typologies.label: Free trade zone abuse for illicit trade and financial crime

citations.quote: Free trade zones, usually located near transport hubs such as ports, offer exemptions from national import and export duties
They become attractive for criminals involved in the trade in illicit goods and financial crime.
Irregular migrants paid between EUR 3 000 and EUR 5 000 per person, depending on the provided services, directly to hawala offices, also in cryptocurrencies.
from informal value transfer systems to the exploitation of cryptocurrencies

typologies.label: Shared professional launderers linking organised-crime proceeds to terrorist financing

citations.quote: Money laundering constitutes the strongest link between these milieus, as several cases of laundering of organised crime proceeds have been associated with the financing of terrorism.
The same professional money laundering service providers often operate as connectors between the worlds.

actors.name: Professional money launderers and money brokers
actors.role: Specialised launderers and high-level brokers offering unregulated financial services to multiple criminal networks, increasingly skilled in digital asset trading

citations.quote: Money laundering can be conducted either by those directly involved in the predicate offence or by specialised professional money launderers and brokers.

actors.name: ChipMixer
actors.role: Unlicensed cryptocurrency mixer taken down March 2023; may have laundered 152 000 Bitcoins linked to darkweb markets, ransomware and Hydra Market

citations.quote: The investigation into the criminal service suggests that the platform may have facilitated the laundering of 152 000 Bitcoins (worth roughly EUR 2.73 billion in current estimations) in crypto assets.

actors.name: Hybrid threat actors
actors.role: States and state-aligned actors using criminal networks as proxies, outsourcing cyber-attacks, disinformation and money laundering for deniability; sanctions evasion strengthens them

citations.quote: It also allows these states to deny direct involvement by outsourcing certain crimes such as cyber-attacks, disinformation campaigns or even money laundering to criminal networks, making attribution difficult.
The evasion of sanctions not only contributes to economic destabilisation; it also indirectly fuels hybrid threats by strengthening sanctioned economies and foreign powers.

actors.name: Dutch military-goods export network
actors.role: Three individuals arrested early 2024 for shipping aircraft parts and military equipment to Russian entities via front companies and falsified documents

citations.quote: uncovered that the suspects had shipped aircraft parts and other military equipment to Russian entities.

actors.name: EUR 297 million VAT fraud network
actors.role: Around 400 companies across 15 Member States selling EUR 1.48 billion of electronics online, missing-trader VAT loss of EUR 297 million, proceeds moved offshore

citations.quote: The suspects established multiple companies in 15 Member States, which acted as legitimate suppliers of electronic goods.
The proceeds of this criminal activity were then transferred to offshore accounts.

actors.name: JuicyFields investment fraud network
actors.role: Cannabis-cultivation Ponzi scheme, ~EUR 645 million reported damage, led by Russian masterminds with strawmen in Germany and laundering in Cyprus

citations.quote: In the “JuicyFields” investment fraud case, suspects lured victims into fraudulent crowdsourcing investments in the cultivation and distribution of cannabis for medicinal purposes.

actors.name: Russian criminal networks
actors.role: Expected to expand operations and financial networks through money laundering across Europe in a post-war or sanctions-lifting scenario

citations.quote: The lifting of economic sanctions on Russia, should it accompany a peace settlement, could also allow Russian criminal networks to enhance their financial networks through money laundering, and criminal finances across Europe or beyond.

actors.name: Thieves in Law
actors.role: Named Eurasian criminal fraternity whose future depends on how the war in Ukraine ends

citations.quote: The future of the Thieves in Law (Vory v Zakone) will also depend on how the war in Ukraine ends and how power shifts within Russia, Ukraine, and the broader criminal underworld.

actors.name: Greek counterfeit-goods network owning courier companies
actors.role: Sold counterfeit luxury goods online, EUR 18 million laundered via businesses it owned, including two courier companies exchanging goods and money to conceal activity

citations.quote: The criminal network had managed to distribute over 364 000 parcels to customers and obtain more than EUR 18 million in illicit profits, laundered via other business companies owned by the network.

actors.name: Morocco–Spain cannabis helicopter network
actors.role: Trafficked cannabis by helicopter from Morocco to Spain and onward to France; used false identities and shell companies to launder the profits

citations.quote: A criminal network used modified helicopters to traffic cannabis from Morocco to the South of Spain.

actors.name: LockBit
actors.role: Ransomware-as-a-service operation disrupted February 2024; ransoms in cryptocurrency split between core team and affiliates

citations.quote: In February 2024, law enforcement from 10 countries disrupted the LockBit ransomware, causing billions of euros worth of damage.

actors.name: Money mules (young and vulnerable recruits)
actors.role: Young people recruited via social media and gaming platforms to receive and transfer illicit funds through their bank accounts

citations.quote: Young people are used as money mules, receiving and transferring illicit funds through their bank accounts, often in exchange for a small share of the money.

extraction_notes: Golden label. Scoped to financial-crime typologies only: fraud crime areas (investment, BEC, romance, payment-system fraud), corruption, drugs, THB, cyber, CSE and firearms are not labelled as typologies even though they dominate the page count; MTIC/VAT fraud is kept because it is a corporate-structure and trade scheme. SAN006 chosen over TBML010 per the twin convention; SAN007 at medium because the text says 'military-grade' and 'strategic' goods, never 'dual-use'. TBML001 not labelled: 'trade misinvoicing' (p25) and 'inflating the price of waste' (p65) are single mentions. PAT004 Circular Ownership not labelled; the carousel is circular TRADE (TBML006). Cash couriers (p25) mentioned once, not labelled. LockBit and hybrid threat actors kept as actors because ransom payments in crypto and outsourced laundering are named; Hydra Market folded into ChipMixer's role. Ukraine is a risk location here (drug labs, firearms source, post-war), not only a victim state. Eurasian Economic Union, Caucasus, West/Central Asia and Western Balkans have no ISO code and are omitted.
